apollonian-dionysian: In The Birth of Tragedy, Nietzsche names two opposing drives in Greek art. The Apollonian, after the god of light and dreams, is the drive toward order, form, boundaries, and self-control; the Dionysian, after the god of wine, is the drive toward intoxication, chaos, and dissolving into ecstatic unity. Nietzsche held Greek tragedy was born of their fusion, and the pair now names any tension between structure and unruly energy.
argument-from-reason: An argument made famous by C. S. Lewis: if naturalism is true — if our beliefs are just products of irrational physical causes — then we have no reason to trust our own reasoning, including the reasoning behind naturalism itself. So, on this view, rational thought cannot be a purely natural process and points to a rational source behind the world. Critics, notably Elizabeth Anscombe, dispute whether this follows.
aristotle-soul: For Aristotle, the soul (psyche) is not a ghost in a machine but the 'form' of a living body — the set of capacities that makes it alive. He ranks them: plants nourish themselves, animals also sense and move, humans additionally reason. Soul and body are, on this view, inseparable in ordinary life, so the soul is not something that simply floats free of the flesh.
augustine-time: In his Confessions, Augustine finds time baffling: the past no longer exists, the future does not yet exist, and the present, to be real, would have to be an instant with no length at all. Yet we plainly measure time and feel it pass. His solution: time exists in the mind, as memory, attention, and expectation — three 'presents' rather than three separate times.
berkeley-idealism: The view of the eighteenth-century philosopher George Berkeley, summed up in esse est percipi: 'to be is to be perceived.' An ordinary object is nothing over and above the ideas — colors, shapes, tastes — that perceivers have of it; there is no hidden, mind-independent matter underneath. Berkeley argued this defeats skepticism, and that things keep existing unperceived because God perceives them always.
catharsis: Aristotle's term in the Poetics for what tragedy does to its audience: by arousing pity and fear for the suffering hero, a play brings about a catharsis of those emotions — a purging, purification, or clarification (translators disagree) that leaves us unburdened rather than corrupted. This answers Plato's charge that drama merely whips up dangerous feelings. Today the word also names any safe emotional release through art.
compatibilism: The view that free will and determinism can both be true. Compatibilists hold that being free does not mean escaping causation; it means acting from your own desires, values, and reasons, without external compulsion. On this account a choice can be fully caused and still genuinely yours, so moral responsibility survives even if everything we do has prior causes. Critics reply that this is freedom in name only.
cosmopolitanism-ethics: The view that every person belongs to a single moral community of humankind, not just to their own nation — a 'citizen of the world,' as the ancient Cynic Diogenes put it. Cosmopolitans hold that duties to strangers are real, even if many allow special obligations to family and compatriots too. In politics it supports human rights and cooperation across borders, against the idea that morality stops at the frontier.
descartes-cogito: René Descartes's foundation for knowledge. Doubting everything he could — the senses, his body, even whether he was dreaming — he found one thing doubt could not touch: the very act of doubting proved that he, the thinker, existed. 'I think, therefore I am' thus became his indubitable starting point, from which he built knowledge of a thinking mind distinct from matter. Later philosophers question how much it supports.
extended-mind: The thesis, proposed by Andy Clark and David Chalmers, that the mind is not confined to the skull. When a tool — a notebook, a phone, a wearable device — is reliably available, constantly used, and trusted the way we trust memory, it can count as part of your mind rather than an aid to it. The idea belongs to the thought that cognition spreads across brains, bodies, and environments.
forgiveness: The deliberate release of resentment toward someone who has wronged you, for moral reasons — not because the wrong was excused, justified, or forgotten. Philosophers debate its conditions: does forgiveness require the offender's repentance or apology? Is it always a virtue, or can it be premature, or even a betrayal of other victims? Most agree it differs from merely pardoning, condoning, or moving on.
hegel-master-slave: A famous episode in Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit. Two self-conscious beings meet, each wanting recognition from the other, and their struggle hardens into a relation of master and slave. Paradoxically, the master, dependent on unequal acknowledgment, gains nothing, while the slave, shaped by labor on the world, gradually achieves genuine selfhood. The story became a template for thinking about domination and mutual recognition, influencing Marx, Fanon, and many others.
incongruity-theory-humor: The leading philosophical theory of what makes things funny: we laugh when something violates expectation or fits no familiar pattern — a mismatch between setup and outcome. Kant and Schopenhauer gave it classic form: laughter comes from the sudden collapse of a strained expectation. Critics note it needs supplementing, since a broken expectation can shock rather than amuse, and much humor never gets resolved.
locke-personal-identity: John Locke's proposal that a person is the same over time in virtue of continuity of consciousness, not of having the same body or soul. On his view, you are the person you remember being: memory links your present self to your past ones. The theory faces puzzles — circularity, forgotten crimes, false memories — but it set the terms for centuries of debate about what makes you you.
logical-positivism: A movement of the 1920s–30s Vienna Circle holding that a statement is meaningful only if it is true by definition or empirically testable. Its verifiability principle dismissed much traditional metaphysics and theology as not merely false but literally meaningless. The principle proved hard to state without destroying itself, and the movement was largely abandoned by mid-century — yet it shaped what analytic philosophy has counted as rigorous ever since.
minimal-state: Robert Nozick's view, in Anarchy, State, and Utopia, that the only legitimate state is one limited to protecting citizens against force, theft, fraud, and breach of contract — nothing more. Anything beyond that, including taxation to fund welfare, violates individual rights; Nozick likens redistributive taxation to forced labor. Libertarians embrace this as the benchmark of freedom; most others reject it as too thin a basis for justice.
panopticon: Jeremy Bentham's eighteenth-century prison design: a ring of cells around a tower from which guards could observe any inmate without the inmates knowing whether they were watched. Michel Foucault made it the emblem of modern power: when people believe they may be observed at any moment, they police themselves, so control works by being internalized rather than by force — a logic he saw spreading through schools, workplaces, and hospitals.
personal-identity: The question of what makes a person at one time the same person at a later time — what your continued survival consists in. Proposed answers include bodily continuity, psychological continuity (memories, character, intentions carried forward), being the same living animal, or a narrative you construct. Thought experiments like imagined teletransporters and brain swaps test them, and Derek Parfit argued the question may have no deep answer.
platonic-love: From Plato's Symposium, where the priestess Diotima describes love as a ladder: we begin by desiring one beautiful body, then come to appreciate all bodily beauty, then the beauty of souls and knowledge, and finally Beauty itself — the form beyond any particular person. Love, on this view, ascends from the physical to the philosophical. The phrase later shifted to mean non-sexual affection, though that is not quite Plato's ladder.
political-animal: Aristotle's claim that the human being is 'by nature a political animal' (zoon politikon): we flourish only in the shared life of a city, not as isolated individuals. Unlike bees, he argued, we have language, which lets us reason together about the just and the unjust — so the state is natural to us, not a mere deal for self-protection among isolated individuals.
possible-worlds: A standard device for talking about how things could have been: a statement is possible if it holds in some 'possible world,' necessary if it holds in all of them. Most philosophers treat possible worlds as useful fictions or abstract constructions. David Lewis, however, defended modal realism — the striking view that every possible world is exactly as real as ours, and ours is the one we happen to inhabit.
social-contract: The idea, developed by Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau, that the state's authority rests on an agreement among individuals who trade some natural liberty for security and order. Each paints the pre-political 'state of nature' differently — for Hobbes a war of all against all, for Locke a state governed by natural law — and each derives different limits on legitimate government. John Rawls recast the contract as a hypothetical choice.
time-travel: In philosophy, less about physics than about logical puzzles: can you change the past, or only take part in it? The grandfather paradox — preventing your existence — suggests incoherence, and David Lewis answers that you can do things in the past but cannot change what in fact happened; whatever you do was already part of history. Other models include fixed timelines, causal loops with no origin, and branching worlds.
truth-in-fiction: The question of what counts as true inside a story. Some truths are stated outright ('Robin is Canadian'); many more are implied — we assume Sherlock Holmes has a heart, though Conan Doyle never says so, since background facts of the world carry over unless overridden. Philosophers like Kendall Walton and David Lewis analyze fiction as a game of make-believe whose truths are what the story instructs us to imagine.
